title: Eyes and Ears
theme: The roots vis/vid and aud: seeing and hearing
objectives: I can use the roots vis (see) and aud (hear) to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can use the prefix in- (not) to explain how invisible and inaudible are built.
I can tell the difference between words about sight and words about sound.
I can write a description of a scene using words about what can be seen and heard.
rationale: Vis and aud are two sense-roots that work in the same way: visible/audible, invisible/inaudible. That symmetry lets students check a meaning against its parts, and it connects to the observation work from earlier in the year (detect, discern, conspicuous, obscure). Four words are about sight in a literal way (visual, invisible, vista, visualize), two reach into the mind (envision, visionary), and four are about sound and listening (audible, inaudible, audience, auditory). Students leave able to decode dozens of other words that carry the same roots.

passage.title: The Play on the Hill
paras: Ms. Brandt was a visionary director. While other teachers planned the spring play for the gym, she looked at the grassy hill behind the school and could envision a stage there, with the whole valley spread out behind the actors. Many parents were doubtful, but when the principal stood at the top and saw the vista of river, bridges, and distant mountains, he agreed.

Planning an outdoor show brought new problems. In the gym, every word had been audible even in the back row. On the hill, wind carried voices away, and when sixth-grader Noor tried her opening line from the middle of the stage, it was almost inaudible. "I can't hear you!" called a friend from the grass.

The cast learned to project their voices, and they also learned to use their bodies. "Audience members will be sitting far away," Ms. Brandt said. "They need a strong visual story, not only words." The actors wore bright costumes, carried big painted props, and used wide gestures. The stagehands wore dark clothes so that, at dusk, they were nearly invisible as they moved the scenery.

Sound mattered, too. Some students were auditory learners who remembered lines best by listening, so they taught everyone songs and rhythms to help the words stick. Before opening night, Ms. Brandt asked the cast to close their eyes and visualize the whole performance, from the first step to the final bow.

On opening night, the audience climbed the hill with blankets and flashlights. When Noor spoke her first line, it carried clearly across the grass. As the sun set behind the actors, the crowd fell silent. At the end, they stood and clapped for a full minute. Ms. Brandt just smiled and looked out at the vista once more. Her vision had become real.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "inaudible" most nearly means
qs.why: Noor's friend calls out that she cannot hear her, so her line was too quiet to be heard.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Brandt say the actors need a strong visual story?
choices: The audience will be sitting far away and may not hear every word.
The actors have not memorized their lines.
The principal asked for a silent play.
The costumes were cheaper than microphones.
qs.why: Voices were carried away by the wind, so costumes and gestures help the faraway audience follow the story.

qs.q: Which detail in paragraph 1 helps you understand the word "vista"?
choices: The spring play was planned for the gym.
The principal saw river, bridges, and distant mountains from the top.
qs.why: The list of river, bridges, and mountains shows a wide, sweeping view, which is what a vista is.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Ms. Brandt was visionary?
choices: She asked the cast to close their eyes before opening night.
She pictured a stage on the hill when other teachers planned the gym.
She told the stagehands to wear dark clothes.
She smiled at the end of the play.
qs.why: A visionary imagines new possibilities, and she saw a stage where others saw only a hill.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Outdoor plays are always better than indoor ones.
Acting is more about costumes than about words.
A big idea needs careful planning and solutions to new problems to come true.
qs.why: Ms. Brandt faces a sound problem, solves it with visual and auditory choices, and makes her vision real.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the roots vis/vid (see) and aud (hear), and see how the prefix in- and the suffix -ible make opposite pairs such as visible/invisible and audible/inaudible. They read a narrative about a play staged on a hillside, practice describing sights and sounds, and write about a place using both senses.

notes.va.visual.adj: Visual relates to sight. Link to the root vis. Students are often told they are visual learners; discuss that this is a preference, not a limit. Ask for three visual aids that help in math.
notes.va.visualize.v: Visualize is forming a mental picture. Practice with a read-aloud passage and have students sketch what they picture. Contrast with envision, which looks ahead.
notes.va.envision.v: Envision is imagining what could be. Break into en- plus vision. Use future-focused prompts: What do you envision for your school in five years?
notes.va.vista.n: A vista is a wide view. Avoid saying it only means mountains; any wide view can be a vista. Use a photograph and have students write one sentence that begins with From the top.
notes.va.visionary.adj: Visionary is an adjective for imaginative thinking about the future (and a noun for the person). Do not confuse with vision as eyesight. Connect to a historical figure who imagined something new.
notes.va.invisible.adj: Build with in- (not), vis (see), and -ible (able to be). Compare with hidden: hidden is covered, invisible is unable to be seen at all. Ask what in nature is invisible but real.
notes.va.audible.adj: Audible is loud enough to be heard. Break into aud (hear) and -ible. Compare with loud: a sound can be audible without being loud.
notes.va.inaudible.adj: Inaudible is too quiet to hear. Show the matching pattern with invisible. Ask students to give two sounds that are inaudible to humans but audible to animals.
notes.va.audience.n: Audience is the people who watch or listen. Use it in writing: Who is your audience? Note that readers of a written text are also an audience.
notes.va.auditory.adj: Auditory relates to hearing. Link to auditorium and to auditory learner. Contrast with visual. Avoid claiming that learning styles are fixed.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see inaudible. The prefix in- means not. The root aud means hear. The ending -ible means able to be. So inaudible means not able to be heard. In the passage, Noor's line was almost inaudible, so the friends on the grass could not hear her. The parts match the meaning.'

Sense boundaries: visionary taught as an adjective with the noun sense in senses; audience taught as people watching or listening, including readers only in the teacher note; the learning-style note in teacher notes avoids claiming that styles are fixed.

Root meanings 'see' for vis/vid and 'hear' for aud are stated as glosses without origin claims. Morph segmentation is omitted for visual, vista, and audience because their endings are not in morphology.json.
